# 2 Maccabees Chapter 12 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic Equivalence)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 12 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_012_page_001.jpg

---

**12:1** Once the agreements were in place, Lysias returned to the king, and the Jews went back to working their land.

**12:2** But certain local officials — Timothy, Apollonius son of Gennaeus, Hieronymus, Demophon, and Nicanor the governor of Cyprus — refused to leave them in peace.

**12:3** The people of Joppa committed a particularly vicious act. They invited the local Jewish community — men, women, and children — to board some boats they had prepared, giving every appearance of friendliness.

**12:4** When the Jews trusted them and went aboard — following what appeared to be an official city decision — the Joppites sailed them out to sea and drowned them all. No fewer than two hundred people died.

**12:5** When Judas heard what had happened to his countrymen, he mobilized his forces.

**12:6** Calling on God, the just judge, he struck at the murderers. He burned the harbor by night, destroyed the boats, and killed those who had fled there.

**12:7** The city gates were shut against him, so he pulled back, planning to return and wipe out the whole community of Joppa once and for all.

**12:8** Then he heard that the people of Jamnia were planning the same thing against the Jews living there.

**12:9** He struck Jamnia by night too — burning the harbor and the fleet. The glow lit up the sky and was visible all the way from Jerusalem, 240 stadia away.

**12:10** As they marched against Timothy, nine stadia down the road from Jamnia, they were ambushed by no fewer than five thousand Arabs and five hundred cavalry.

**12:11** A fierce battle followed. God helped them, and the nomads were beaten. The defeated Arabs came to Judas asking for terms, promising to supply cattle and to help them in other ways.

**12:12** Judas judged that they could be genuinely useful and agreed to make peace. After the pledges were exchanged, the Arabs withdrew to their camps.

**12:13** Judas also attacked a fortified city called Caspin, surrounded by earthworks and walls, with a mixed population of various peoples.

**12:14** The people inside were confident in their defenses and their supply stockpiles. They mocked Judas and his men with contemptuous insults and said things that were too wicked to repeat.

**12:15** But Maccabeus called on the great Lord of the universe — the same God who, without a single battering ram or siege engine, had knocked down the walls of Jericho for Joshua — and flung himself against the wall.

**12:16** By God's will the city fell. The slaughter that followed was beyond description. The lake nearby, two stadia wide, looked as if it were running over with blood.

**12:17** They marched 750 stadia further and came to Charax, where the Jews known as the Tubiani lived.

**12:18** Timothy was not there. He had already cleared out without having accomplished anything — though he had left a strong garrison at one position.

**12:19** Two of Maccabeus's commanders, Dositheus and Sosipater, attacked the garrison and destroyed it — more than ten thousand soldiers.

**12:20** Maccabeus reorganized his army into divisions, put those commanders in charge of them, and moved fast to catch Timothy, who had assembled 120,000 infantry and 2,500 cavalry.

**12:21** When Timothy got word that Judas was coming, he sent the women, children, and baggage ahead to Carnaim — a place that was extremely hard to besiege because all its approaches were narrow and difficult.

**12:22** But when the lead division of Judas's army came into view, the enemy was seized with terror. They knew what it meant when God — who sees everything — showed his hand, and they broke and ran in every direction. In their panic, they injured each other and impaled themselves on their own swords.

**12:23** Judas pursued them relentlessly and cut down the guilty — some thirty thousand in all.

**12:24** Timothy himself fell into the hands of Dositheus, Sosipater, and their men. Timothy was clever — he begged them to spare his life, claiming he was holding the parents of most of them and the brothers of some as prisoners, and that these relatives would be killed if anything happened to him.

**12:25** When he gave full assurances that the hostages would be returned safely, they let him go rather than risk the lives of their families.

**12:26** Judas then attacked Carnaim and the temple of Atargatis, and killed twenty-five thousand people.

**12:27** After this victory, he moved against Ephron, a fortified city with a large and mixed population. Its defenders — strong young men — took their positions at the walls and put up a fierce fight. The city had plenty of war machines and ammunition.

**12:28** Calling on the Lord, who shatters the power of enemies, they took the city and killed twenty-five thousand of its people.

**12:29** From there they marched to Scythopolis, 600 stadia from Jerusalem.

**12:30** The Jews who lived in Scythopolis spoke up for the city — the Scythopolitans had shown genuine kindness to their community and treated them well during the bad times.

**12:31** After thanking them and urging them to remain good friends to the Jewish people in the future, they headed back to Jerusalem. The feast of Weeks was approaching.

**12:32** After the festival of Pentecost, they moved out quickly against Gorgias, the governor of Idumea.

**12:33** Gorgias came out to meet them with three thousand infantry and four hundred cavalry.

**12:34** When battle was joined, a small number of Jews were killed.

**12:35** A soldier named Dositheus, from Bacenor's cavalry — a powerful man — got hold of Gorgias himself, grabbed his cloak, and was hauling him away. But a Thracian rider came up and slashed off Dositheus's arm at the shoulder. Gorgias escaped to Marisa.

**12:36** Esdris and his men had been fighting a long time and were exhausted. Judas called on the Lord to show himself as their champion and leader.

**12:37** He launched the attack with a battle cry in Hebrew and with hymns, catching Gorgias's forces off guard and routing them.

**12:38** Judas regrouped his forces and moved to the town of Adullam. As the seventh day was coming on, they purified themselves in the customary way and kept the Sabbath there.

**12:39** The next day, as was now necessary, Judas's men went out to recover the bodies of the fallen and bring them home to be buried with their ancestors.

**12:40** But when they turned out the bodies, they found something shocking: under the tunic of every fallen soldier were amulets sacred to the idols of Jamnia — objects the law explicitly forbids Jews to wear. It was now obvious to everyone why these men had died.

**12:41** They all praised the Lord, the righteous judge who brings hidden things to light.

**12:42** Then they turned to prayer, begging God to wipe out the sin completely. Judas the noble urged the people to keep themselves from sin — what had happened was a stark and terrible lesson.

**12:43** He took up a collection, man by man, raising two thousand drachmas in silver, and sent it to Jerusalem to pay for a sin offering on behalf of the dead. It was a beautiful and honorable act — done in full view of the resurrection of the dead.

**12:44** For if he had no hope that the fallen would rise again, it would have been pointless and absurd to pray for the dead.

**12:45** But if he believed in the glorious reward waiting for those who die in faithfulness to God, then his concern for them was holy and right. And so he made atonement for the dead, that they might be set free from their sin.
